```{r setup, include=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(lsa)

```

### 1. Data Pre-Processing for "Binary" Data

The downloaded data came in the form of an Excel workbook (.xls) with three different tabs: 

1. "Binary"  :  Spreadsheet containing dichotomous scoring of correct (coded as "1") and wrong (coded as "0") answers
2. "Answers" :  Spreadsheet containing the actual L1 translations keyed in by the participants
3. "Times"   :  Spreadsheet containing reaction times it took to answer each test item

Therefore, there is a need to process the files and concatenate them into one large dataframe before any further analysis. Since the all the sheets in each Excel Workbook follow the same data structure, it is possible to concatenate the files while maintaining the integrity of the row and column positions. 

The following are the steps that were taken:

* Step 1: Turn all relevant spreadsheets into individual .csv files
* Step 2: Converting files into R-readable format by removing irrelevant rows and columns in each .csv file
* Step 3: Add unique IDs to each row in every .csv file
* Step 4: Concatenate all .csv files into one big dataframe


```{r binary-one-big-df, eval=FALSE}

#### Step 1: Convert "Binary" sheets into csv ####

# Set input and output directories
input_dir <- "M:/receptivedata"
output_dir <- "M:/binary-csv"

# List all Excel files (.xlsx and .xls)
excel_files <- list.files(path = input_dir, pattern = "\\.xls[x]?$", full.names = TRUE)

# Loop through each Excel file
for (file in excel_files) {
  
  # Read the sheet with binary data
  df <- read_excel(file, sheet = "Binary")
  
  # Create the output CSV file name
  file_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
  output_file <- file.path(output_dir, paste0(file_name, ".csv"))
  
  # Write to CSV
  write.csv(df, output_file, row.names = FALSE)
  
  # Print progress
  cat("Converted:", basename(file), "\n")
}



#### Step 2: Converting all .csv files into R-readable dataframe ####

# Set input and output directories
input_dir <- "M:/binary-csv"
output_dir <- "M:/binary-rremoved"

# List all CSV files
csv_files <- list.files(path = input_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

# Loop over each CSV file
for (file in csv_files) {
  
  # Read the CSV file
  df <- read.csv(file)
  names(df) <- NULL

  # Remove specific rows by index (e.g., rows 1-17 and 19-22)
  df_rremoved <- df[-c(1:16, 18:21), -c(3:4)]
  
  # Create an output file name
  # output_file <- file.path(path = output_dir, file)
  file_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
  output_file <- file.path(output_dir, paste0(file_name, "_rrm", ".csv"))
  
  # Save the cleaned DataFrame
  write.csv(df_rremoved, output_file, row.names = FALSE)
  
  # Print progress
  cat("Processed:", file, "\n")
}



#### Step 3: Add unique participant IDs ####

## Step 3a: Rename files according to year & month

# Set source and destination directories
source_dir <- "M:/binary-rremoved"
dest_dir <- "M:/binary-renamed"

# List files in the source directory
files <- list.files(source_dir, full.names = TRUE)

# Loop through each file
for (file in files) {
  # Extract base file name and extension
  base <- basename(file)
  name_no_ext <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(base)
  ext <- tools::file_ext(base)
  
  # Truncate to first 6 characters; this is the month of data
  truncated_name <- substr(name_no_ext, 1, 6)
  
  # Combine to create new file name
  new_filename <- paste0(truncated_name, ".", ext)
  new_path <- file.path(dest_dir, new_filename)
  
  # Copy the file with the new name
  file.copy(from = file, to = new_path)
  
  cat("Copied:", base, "->", new_filename, "\n")
}



## Step 3b: Add participant IDs using year & month on file name

# Set directory to make code more readable
source_dir <- "M:/binary-renamed"
new_dir <- "M:/binary-add-id"

# List all CSV files
files <- list.files(path = source_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

# Loop over each CSV file
for (file in files) {
  
  # Extract base file name and remove extension
  base <- basename(file)
  name_no_ext <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(base)
  
  # Read the CSV file
  df <- read.csv(file)
  
  for (i in nrow(df)){
    df[,1] <- paste0(name_no_ext, df[,1])
  }
  output_file <- file.path(new_dir)
  write.csv(df, file=paste0(new_dir,base), row.names = FALSE)
}



#### Step 4: Concatenate all edited csv files into one big dataframe ####

# Note: Item ID is consistent across the months, so dataframes can be concatenated using bind_rows()
# Set directory 
source_dir <- "M:/binary-add-id"

# List all files
files <- list.files(path = source_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

# Bind all dfs
df <- bind_rows(lapply(files, read.csv))

write.csv(df, "all_binary.csv", row.names = FALSE)



### 2. Removing rows & columns with only NA values

# Load dataframe
df <- read.csv("M:/all_binary_foriegn_id_filtered.csv")
# N = 45774 observations

# Remove rows with only "NA" values
df <- df[!apply(is.na(df), 1, all), ]
# N = 45774; no observations removed. Looks like the empty rows are all the known CN L1 students who were already removed from the system previously

# Remove columns with only "NA" values
df <- df[, !apply(is.na(df), 2, all)]
# K = 8008 (df has 8009 variables); full list of test items was K = 8149 (i.e., 8150 variables), so 141 test items had only NAs

# Remove rows with only value "1" to look for invalid responses from system testing
df <- df[!apply(df == 1, 1, all), ]
# N = 45774; no observations removed. Looks like any system testing (if included) did not use all items at any one time

# Rename first column
names(df)[1] <- "id"

# Write file to .csv
write.csv(df, "all_binary_atleast1.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

### 3. Filtering out all rows with non-Japanese respondents

Next, the actual answers provided by respondents will be used to remove any potential non-Japanese L1 participants. 

#### 3a. Testing with generated data 

* Prior to running the code to filter the actual data, the code was tested with generated data first.

```{r answers-filter-toy-data, eval=FALSE}

# Trial run of filtering process using made-up data
# Set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Create example Japanese and non-Japanese text
japanese_text <- c("こんにちは", "~ありがとう", "さようなら", "テスト", "日本語")
non_japanese_text <- c("hello", "world", "data", "science", "example")
kanji_text <- c("日本語", "信頼", "横浜", "你好", "再见")

# Function to generate random values: Japanese, non-Japanese, or NA
generate_mixed_value <- function() {
  choices <- c(japanese_text, non_japanese_text, NA)
  sample(choices, 1)
}

# Generate a 20x20 dataframe
df <- as.data.frame(
  matrix(nrow = 20, ncol = 20, data = replicate(20*20, generate_mixed_value()))
)

# Create 5 rows with only Japanese and NA values
generate_japanese_or_na <- function() {
  choices <- c(japanese_text, NA)
  sample(choices, 20, replace = TRUE)
}

df_japanese_na <- as.data.frame(
  t(replicate(5, generate_japanese_or_na()))
)


# Create 5 rows with only English and NA values
generate_english_or_na <- function() {
  choices <- c(non_japanese_text, NA)
  sample(choices, 20, replace = TRUE)
}

df_english_na <- as.data.frame(
  t(replicate(5, generate_english_or_na()))
)


# Create 5 rows with only Kanji and NA values
generate_kanji_or_na <- function() {
  choices <- c(kanji_text, NA)
  sample(choices, 20, replace = TRUE)
}

df_kanji_na <- as.data.frame(
  t(replicate(5, generate_kanji_or_na()))
)


# Combine dataframes
df_combined <- rbind(df, df_japanese_na, df_english_na, df_kanji_na, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
# Now, we have a dataframe containing a mix of JP script, EN script, and NAs


# Regex patterns: to capture every row that does not contain Japanese script
jp_script <- "[\\p{Han}\\p{Hiragana}\\p{Katakana}\\～~∼０-９\\0-9]"
non_jp_script <- "[^\\p{Han}\\p{Hiragana}\\p{Katakana}\\～~∼]"

# Testing: filtering non-JP script
filtered_non_jp_rows <- df_combined %>%
  filter(
    apply(., 1, function(row) {
      all(is.na(row) | grepl(non_jp_script, row, perl = TRUE))
    })
  )
# As expected, the filter removed everything except "only-English" rows
# "Kanji-only" rows are included in the filter


# Testing: filtering JP script
filtered_jp_rows <- df_combined %>%
  filter(
    apply(., 1, function(row) {
      all(is.na(row) | grepl(jp_script, row, perl = TRUE))
    })
  )
# As expected, this included all the rows with Chinese characters (aka Kanji) too
# The "tilda" sign is included coz JP students tend to use this for some function words to indicate their syntactic function

```

#### 3b. Filtering the actual data for L1 JP respondents only

* After rounds of initial testing using the generated data, the actual filtering takes the following steps:
    
    
    1. Filter out responses with strictly JP script only
    2. Filter for any potential CN respondents, since the regex pattern does not differentiate CN from JP kanji
    3. Export lists without NAs for visual inspection


```{r answers-JPonly-filter, eval=FALSE}

# Filter for strictly JP-only rows

# Load dataframe
df_all_ans <- read.csv("M:/all-answers.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# N = 45965, K = 8150

# JP pattern regex
jp_script <- "[\\p{Han}\\p{Hiragana}\\p{Katakana}\\<ok\\>\\<OK\\>\\s\\～~∼ー?？xX✕ｘ❌０-９\\0-9]"
# Note that some non-JP symbols are included because some JP students tend to use them

# Filtering JP-only script
filtered_jp_only <- df_all_ans %>%
  filter(
    apply(., 1, function(row) {
      all(is.na(row) | grepl(jp_script, row, perl = TRUE))
    })
  )
# N = 45073; 892 observations containing non-JP script removed; this is a strict filter where responses with any English alphabets will be removed 
# N = 44929 without words "ok" and "OK"

# Note that this filtered list may contain CN respondents

# Export JP-only dataframe as .csv
write.csv(filtered_jp_only, "jp_answers.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

#### 3c. Filtering for any potential CN respondents

* Since JP and CN share the same encoding for kanji scripts, this chunk of code is for removing any potential CN participants 
* Four different approaches were used, and none of them yielded any CN respondents
* Thus, it is safe to say that the dataset is very unlikely to contain L1 Chinese respondents


```{r answers-remove-CN, eval=FALSE}

# To further remove potential CN respondents by using CN-only script
df <- read.csv("M:/preprocessing-working-file_20251201/jp_answers.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)


#METHOD 1: Filter for responses that contain nothing but kanji
# Define regex pattern for kanji
kanji <- "[\\p{Han}]"

# Filtering only Kanji script (to identify Chinese L1 speakers)
filtered_kanji_only <- df %>%
  filter(
    apply(., 1, function(row) {
      all(is.na(row) | grepl(kanji, row, perl = TRUE))
    })
  )
# Filtering for kanji-only responses for CN respondents returned zero observations



# METHOD 2: List CN-only characters using UTF-8 and filter them out
cn_script_raw <- readLines("M:/cn_only_utf8_reduced.txt", encoding = "UTF-8") #truncated the list to around 900 characters
cn_script_chr <- stringi::stri_split_boundaries(cn_script_raw, type="character")
cn_script <- paste(cn_script_chr, collapse = "|")
cn_script
# Filtering with UTF-8 encoded CN-only characters returned zero observations



# METHOD 3: Manual listing of low frequency CN characters that are also used as JP kanji
cn_script_test <- "[\\你\\我\\他\\她\\它\\谁\\的\\们\\门]"
# Filtering with manual list of common CN characters that are shared with JP returned zero observations
# Random words tested with search function in Excel but returned zero observations



# METHOD 4: Use DeepL CN-only translations of test items and filtering for them to maximize likelihood of catching any CN observations
# All specifically-CN translations are broken into 9 lists of ~990 lines due to RAM limitations
# Full list of k = 7341 one-word items is in Excel file with item id, and test items in English, Japanese, and Chinese

cn_ans_raw <- readLines("M:/cn_answers9.txt", encoding = "UTF-8")
cn_ans <- paste(cn_ans_raw, collapse = "|")

# Filtering for CN translations of items answers in English
filtered_cn <- df %>%
  filter(
    apply(., 1, function(row) {
      all(is.na(row) | grepl(cn_ans, row, perl = TRUE))
    })
  )

# The last list "cn_answers9.txt" returned 417 observations
# To filter out the actual answers for each row and concatenate them as a string and paste in a new column to see what is filtered out
filtered_cn$non_na_values <- apply(filtered_cn, 1, function(row) {
  row[!is.na(row)]
})
filtered_cn$non_na_values <- lapply(filtered_cn$non_na_values, unname)
# These are all just empty columns; for some reason R reads the .txt and filtered out all responses with nothing but NAs in the answer sheet

# To keep a record and cross check if these 417 observations coincide with all filtered invalid responses later
# Create empty dataframe
cn_empty_list <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = 0, nrow = 417))

# Copy and paste list to new dataframe
cn_empty_list$ans <- filtered_cn$non_na_values
cn_empty_df <- as.data.frame(rbind(cn_empty_list))

writeLines(as.character(cn_empty_df), "cn_empty_ids.txt")
# Method 4 also yielded zero observations

```

### 4. Visual check for the filtered non-JP scripts in the "Answer" data

* The non-JP answers were filtered for a quick visual check
* A sample of the removed responses are below. It appears that there might be legitimate responses that were removed because response contains at least 1 English alphabet and/or emojis


    + However, this is ok since it is better to have a stricter filter than a lenient filter, which has a higher likelihood of including non-Japanese responses


```{r answers-visualise-nonJP, eval=FALSE}

# Load all answers
df_all_ans <- read.csv("all-answers.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
filtered_jp_only <- read.csv("jp_answers.csv", , fileEncoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Filter for non-JP respondents (n = 892)
non_jp_ans <- dplyr::anti_join(df_all_ans, filtered_jp_only, by=c("id"))


# Truncate all non-NA values by column and convert into list format
non_jp_ans$non_na_values <- apply(non_jp_ans, 1, function(row) {
  row[!is.na(row)]
})
non_jp_ans$non_na_values <- lapply(non_jp_ans$non_na_values, unname)

# Create empty dataframe
non_jp_ans_df <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = 0, nrow = 892))

# Copy and paste list to new dataframe
non_jp_ans_df$ans <- non_jp_ans$non_na_values
non_jp_ans_list_df <- as.data.frame(rbind(non_jp_ans_df))

# Export the non-JP files
writeLines(as.character(non_jp_ans_list_df), "nonjp_ans_list.txt")
write.csv(non_jp_ans, "non_jp_answers.csv", row.names=FALSE)

# The non-JP list appears to potentially contain legitimate JP responses, but student had typed at least one alphabet (apart from "x" or "ok") or emojis.
# All these shall be removed as invalid responses since there isn't a way to reinsert these potentially legitimate JP responses into the dataframe consistently

```

### 5. Data Pre-Processing for "Times" Data 

* The reaction time data is used for filtering out any invalid responses that might have included student cheating or system testing
* A quick visual check with one of the files shows that system test responses result in correct answers in <0.3s
* To use RT for filtering, I need to repeat Steps 1-4 done with "Binary" and "Answers" data and concatenate everything into one big dataframe before any filtering can be done

```{r times-one-big-df, eval=FALSE}

# Concatenate Times sheet into one big df

#### Step 1: Convert into .csv files ####

output_dir <- "M:/times-csv"

# List all Excel files (.xlsx and .xls)

  # Read the sheet with reaction times
  df <- read_excel(file, sheet = "Times")

  # Write to CSV

  # Print progress
  cat("Converted:", basename(file), "\n")
}



#### Step 2: Remove unrelated rows ####

  df <- read.csv(file)
  
  # Make all elements into strings
  df <- as.data.frame(sapply(df, as.character), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  
  # Concatenate dataframe
  big_df <- bind_rows(big_df, df)
}

# Rename first column
names(big_df)[1] <- "id"

# Write to .csv
write.csv(big_df, "all-times.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

### 6. Using reaction times as filter to remove invalid responses

* Now, with all the times concatenated into a large dataframe, the following steps were applied:


    1. Sum row vectors in the all-Binary dataframe to find the total number of correct responses for each respondent
    2. Sum all the values in the all-Times dataframe to find total reaction time
    3. Divide (2) with (1) to find the average reaction time to each correct response
    4. Values below a certain threshold will be used to filter out the responses

* The code was first tested with a toy example before applied to the actual data

```{r rt-filter, eval=FALSE}

#### 1. Testing using toy dataframe ####

# Generate dataframes with ids

# RT dataframe
df_randa <- randu

# Binary dataframe
a <- sample(x = c(0,1), size = 400, replace = TRUE)
b <- sample(x = c(0,1), size = 400, replace = TRUE)
c <- sample(x = c(0,1), size = 400, replace = TRUE)

df_randbin <- as.data.frame(cbind(a,b,c))

# Create "participant" ids
id <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = , nrow = 400))

for (i in 1:400){
    id[i,1] <- paste0(i, collapse="", sep="")
}    

colnames(id) <- "participants"

df_randa$participants <- id$participants
df_randbin$participants <- id$participants


# This is the "filtered" binary dataframe for removing "invalid responses"
df_filtered <- df_randbin[101:300,1:4]


# Next, to concatenate the two dataframes
df_combined <- dplyr::inner_join(df_randa, df_filtered, by="participants")
df_splita <- df_combined[1:3]
df_splitb <- df_combined[5:7]

# Create empty column
df_combined$dot <- NA


# Dot product of row vectors
for(j in 1:200){
  dot_product <- sum(df_splita[j,]*df_splitb[j,])
  df_combined[j,8] <- dot_product
}

# Calculate the sum of each row to obtain mean reaction time for each correct answer
df_combined$correctcount <- rowSums(df_splitb)

# Calculate mean RT per correct answer
df_combined$meanRT <- df_combined$dot / df_combined$correctcount

# Plot distributions of mean RT
hist(df_combined$meanRT)
boxplot(df_combined$meanRT)
# The toy example worked, so the steps are repeated with actual data



#### 2. Obtaining average reaction time per correct answer for response ####

# Load dataframe for both all-times and all-binary
df_binary <- read.csv("M:/all_binary.csv")
df_times <- read.csv("M:/all_times.csv")

# Calculate dot product for each pair of row vectors
df_binary_rvectors <- df_binary[3:8151]
df_times_rvectors <- df_times[2:8150]

# Replace all NAs with 0 for dot product operation
df_binary_rvectors[is.na(df_binary_rvectors)] <- 0
df_times_rvectors[is.na(df_times_rvectors)] <- 0

# Create empty dataframe for inputting dot products
df_dot_products <- data.frame(matrix(nrow=45965))
df_dot_products[,1] <- df_binary[,1]

# Fill empty dataframe with dot products
for(i in 1:45965){
  dot_product <- sum(df_binary_rvectors[i,]*df_times_rvectors[i,])
  df_dot_products[i,2] <- dot_product
}

# Calculate the count of correct answers in each row to obtain mean RT
df_dot_products$correctcount <- rowSums(df_binary_rvectors)

# Calculate mean RT per correct answer
df_dot_products$meanRT <- df_dot_products[,2]/df_dot_products[,3]

# Export the list of mean RT by participants
write.csv(df_dot_products, "rt_by_id.csv", row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(df_binary_rvectors, "binary_rvectors.csv", row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(df_times_rvectors, "times_rvectors.csv", row.names=FALSE)

# Note that the dataframe contains all N = 45965 responses, including the ones that are invalid



#### 3. Next, obtain a description on of the distribution of RTs

# Get description of the distribution of RT
# Load dataframes
df<- read.csv("M:/rt_by_id.csv")
df_non_jp <- read.csv("M:/non_JP_answers.csv")

# List of non-JP responses
df_non_jp_id <- as.data.frame(df_non_jp$id)
df_non_jp_id$is_jp <- 0
names(df_non_jp_id)[1] <- "id"


# Removing non-JP reaction times
df_all_rt <- dplyr::right_join(df_non_jp_id, df, by="id")
df_all_rt$is_jp[is.na(df_all_rt$is_jp)] <- 1

# Check the number of JP respondents
sum(df_all_rt$is_jp)
# N = 45073; number checks out

# Create new dataframe for only JP
df_only_jp <- df_all_rt[df_all_rt$is_jp != 0, ]

# Export dataframes
write.csv(df_all_rt, "all_rt.csv", row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(df_only_jp, "only_jp_rt.csv", row.names=FALSE)

```

Here are the descriptive statistics and plots for reaction times for all responses graded as "correct", including both valid and invalid observations:

```{r rt-descriptive, warning=FALSE, eval=TRUE}

# Load dataframe
df_only_jp <- read.csv("M:/only_jp_rt.csv")

# Distribution of reaction times for JP responses
summary(df_only_jp$meanRT)
boxplot(df_only_jp$meanRT, main = "Boxplot of mean RT per logged session for correct responses")
hist(df_only_jp$meanRT, main = "Histogram of mean RT for correct responses", xlab = "Mean RTs per logged session (before filtering)")

```

In order to reduce potential noise from invalid responses such as overly long RTs from cheating and impossibly short RTs due to system testing, only responses that have an average of between 3s and 14s are kept.


```{r remove-extreme-rt, eval=FALSE}

# Load dataframe
df_only_jp <- read.csv("M:/only_jp_rt.csv")
# N = 45073

# Filter for reaction times falling between 3s and 14s
df_only_jp_filtered <- df_only_jp %>%
  dplyr::filter(between(meanRT, 3, 14))

# Export dataframe
write.csv(df_only_jp_filtered, "only_jp_rt_filtered.csv", row.names=FALSE)

```

Here are the updated descriptive plots of the filtered RTs.

Using this information, a list of invalid logged session are extracted and used to remove all invalid responses in the "Binary" dataframe. Thus, the updated "Binary" dataframe now only contains valid responses that contain reaction times between 3 and 14 seconds for correct answers.

```{r binary-rt-filter, eval=FALSE}

# Load dataframes 
df_binary <- read.csv("M:/all_binary_atleast1.csv") 
# df_binary was already previously filtered for known foreign id, NA-only columns and rows

df_only_jp_filtered <- read.csv("M:/only_jp_rt_filtered.csv")
# Now, to use this list of ids based on JP-script and RT to further clean up binary dataframe

df_binary_rt_jp <- dplyr::inner_join(df_binary, df_only_jp_filtered, by="id")
# N = 42754; this is less than the observations in df_only_jp_filtered (N = 42917), indicating that the earlier filter was able to remove observations that would not otherwise have been removed if only RT and JP-script was used

# Export this RT and JP-script filtered dataframe
write.csv(df_binary_rt_jp, "binary_3_to_14_sec.csv", row.names=FALSE)

```


### 7. Removing test items with very few responses

* Thus far, the filtering is aimed at removing invalid responses (aka logged sessions or row vectors)
* This Step 7 is aimed at getting an idea on the amount of "missingness" per test item by looking at the number of responses each test item received 
* This will help with the decision on how much more further filtering is necessary to remove test items with insufficient responses

```{r visualise-missingness, warning=FALSE, out.width="90%"}

# Load dataframes
data <- read.csv("M:/binary_3_to_14_sec.csv")
df <- data[1:8009]

# Count missingness
df_missingness <- df[,-1]

# Count missingness
missingness <- colSums(is.na(df_missingness))

# Summary table
summary(missingness)

# Histogram
hist_missingness <- hist(missingness, ylim = c(0,4200))
text(x = hist_missingness$mids, y = hist_missingness$counts, labels = hist_missingness$counts, pos = 3, col = "black", cex = 0.8)

# Boxplot
box_missingness <- boxplot(missingness, main = "Boxplot of missingness", horizontal = TRUE)
quartiles <- as.integer(round(box_missingness$stats[,1],2))
text(x = quartiles, y = c(1.05, 1.25, 1.25), labels = quartiles, pos = 3, col = "black", cex = 0.5)

```

<p>
#### Observations:

* Minimum no. of missing observations is 40348; i.e., max no. of observations an item has is 42754-40348 = 2406 responses
* Median no. of missing observations is 42601; i.e., median no. of observations an item has is 42754-42601 = 153 responses
* This means filtering out data with less than 153 responses will cut the number of test items in roughly half to around 3500 to 4000 items
</p>

Thus, taking reference from KVL, items with less than 120 responses were removed:

```{r count-per-item-responses, eval=FALSE}

# Load dataframes and transpose for removing items
data <- read.csv("E:/binary_3_to_14_sec.csv")
df <- data[2:8009]

transpose_headings <- as.data.frame(colnames(df))
names(transpose_headings)[1] <- "item_id"

# Replace all NAs with 0 to speed up the process
df[is.na(df)] <- 0

# Transpose the dataframe; found out the hard way this is the better option
df_t <- as.data.frame(t(df))
df_items <- cbind(transpose_headings, df_t)

# Count the number of responses per test item
df_items$responsecounts <- rowSums(df_t[,2:42754])

# Export this information!
write.csv(df_items, "all_item_response_counts.csv", row.names=FALSE)

# Duplicate dataframe
df_t120 <- df_items

# Remove items with less than 120 responses
df_t120 <- df_t120[df_t120$responsecounts >= 120, ]
# Note that I can't use this dataframe to compute cosine similarity directly since all NAs are replaced with 0

# Export this dataframe
write.csv(df_t120, "item_w_120responses.csv", row.names=FALSE)
```

Below displays a description of the distribution of responses per item.
* Note that removing items with less than 120 responses has cut the total number of test items to k = 3013

```{r filtered-items-summary, warning=FALSE, eval=TRUE}

# Load dataframe
df_t120 <- read.csv("M:/item_w_120responses.csv")

# Now, to check out the distribution of responses per item
summary(df_t120$responsecounts)
hist(df_t120$responsecounts)
boxplot(df_t120$responsecounts)

```
<p>

### 8. Potential issue with repeat individuals

* Notes:


    + Usually, multiple responses from the same individual could be considered as "harmless" to IRT models, especially if test-takers respond to different test items that are randomized at each logged session 
    + However, if the same individual does the exact same test at each repetition, this could violate assumptions of observational independence and lead to model overfitting
    + While this model overfitting is unlikely to be an issue, it is better to test what its implications are prior to applying IRT modelling, and see if it is possible or necessary to try accounting for it to reduce potential estimate inaccuracies
